title: A Room for the Bell
premise: Folklorist Sable Villalobos returns to her grandmother's isolated village to record a funeral lament that locals refuse to sing twice, armed with skepticism and a tape recorder. But every photograph in the old house begins showing an extra chair at the table, and the villagers' evasions reveal that decades ago someone invited 'the Bell' inside—a presence that claims one household per generation and erases whoever hears its toll twice. As night falls and the chair draws nearer, Sable learns her grandmother's silence was protection, not superstition: Sable herself was promised to the Bell before she was born. To survive until sunrise she must choose between exposing the village's complicity—destroying the only family she has left—and accepting the identity they forged for her, ending with her singing the lament a second time to bind the Bell to herself on her own terms.
about_author: Felix Sterling is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing oral histories in remote mountain communities before turning those half-heard songs into fiction. They write horror about the debts families hide in plain sight.

chapters.title: The Lament No One Sings Twice
chapters.summary: Sable arrives in the fog-bound village of Corvo Alto with recording equipment and academic confidence. At the wake for old Marta, the mourners sing a lament once, then fall silent when she asks for a second take. POV: Sable. Beat: curiosity sharpening into unease.

chapters.title: Grandmother's House, Full of Chairs
chapters.summary: Sable settles into her late grandmother's house, cataloguing folk artifacts. Reviewing photos of the kitchen, she notices an extra wooden chair that appears in images from different decades. POV: Sable. Beat: rational explanation begins to strain.

chapters.title: What the Archivist Keeps
chapters.summary: In town, Sable interviews Father Anselmo, who deflects questions about the lament but warns her not to play recordings after dark. She finds her grandmother's sealed letters in the parish archive. POV: Sable. Beat: first real dread beneath professional detachment.

chapters.title: The Chair in Every Picture
chapters.summary: Comparing forty years of family photographs, Sable maps the chair's slow approach across rooms toward the head of the table. Her cousin Teo begs her to burn the photos. POV: Sable, with Teo's testimony. Beat: loyalty and truth begin to pull apart.

chapters.title: Songs Under Seal
chapters.summary: Teo confesses the village sings the lament once as warning, never twice as invitation. He reveals his own mother vanished the year he turned nine, and no one speaks of it. POV: Teo. Beat: grief and complicity entwined.

chapters.title: Playback at Midnight
chapters.summary: Defying warnings, Sable plays her recording alone; the tape continues past where she stopped it, a second voice humming underneath. The extra chair is now physically in the kitchen. POV: Sable. Beat: skepticism collapses into terror.

chapters.title: The Bell Registry
chapters.summary: In grandmother's locked chest, Sable finds a ledger listing households and dates—one name per generation, each followed by a blackened entry. The last page bears her own name, dated tomorrow. POV: Sable. Beat: identity becomes a sentence.

chapters.title: Villagers at the Gate
chapters.summary: The village council arrives demanding the ledger back, offering to 'handle things' if she leaves before dark. Their kindness curdles into threat. POV: Sable. Beat: the price of survival made explicit.

chapters.title: Father Anselmo's Confession
chapters.summary: Anselmo admits the church has recorded Bell-takings for two centuries and chose silence to keep the village alive. He gives her a key to the bell tower and a rite half-erased from the records. POV: Anselmo. Beat: institutional guilt, fragile alliance.

chapters.title: Teo's Bargain
chapters.summary: Teo offers to take Sable's place using a blood-debt his family still owes, insisting she deserves the life they stole. Sable refuses, furious that everyone keeps deciding her fate for her. POV: Teo. Beat: love weaponized as sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Photograph That Moves
chapters.summary: Alone again, Sable watches the newest photo change in real time—the chair now occupied by a figure wearing her grandmother's shawl. It raises one finger to its lips. POV: Sable. Beat: intimate horror; the dead are complicit too.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Reading the erased rite, Sable learns the truth: her grandmother invited the Bell in to spare Sable's infant life during a fever year, deferring the debt to her adulthood. Protection was the trap. POV: Sable. Beat: betrayal and gratitude fused.

chapters.title: Sunset Toll
chapters.summary: The distant bell sounds once though the tower has no rope. Doors slam throughout the village; the council seals their own homes, leaving Sable's house outside the salt line. POV: multiple villagers briefly, then Sable. Beat: abandonment crystallizes.

chapters.title: The Long Hour
chapters.summary: Trapped inside, Sable endures the house rearranging itself—hallways lengthening, the chair scraping closer room by room. She records everything, clinging to her archivist's discipline as armor. POV: Sable. Beat: endurance as character.

chapters.title: Voices in the Walls
chapters.summary: The taken speak through the walls—Marta, Teo's mother, generations of names from the ledger—all singing fragments of the lament, teaching it to her whether she wants to learn or not. POV: Sable. Beat: horror turning strangely tender.

chapters.title: Teo Breaks the Salt Line
chapters.summary: Teo returns against the council's will to force the substitution ritual; the house takes him instead, dragging him toward the chair. Sable must choose: let him be claimed or intervene. POV: alternating Sable/Teo. Beat: loyalty tested at maximum cost.

chapters.title: The Second Verse
chapters.summary: Sable pulls Teo free by singing the lament's forbidden second verse—the binding, not the invitation—which stops the Bell mid-motion. The tower key burns cold in her pocket. POV: Sable. Beat: agency seized through inherited knowledge.

chapters.title: Climb to the Tower
chapters.summary: Carrying the ledger and the rite, Sable crosses the frozen village to the bell tower while the Bell manifests as a procession of empty chairs rolling through the streets behind her. POV: Sable. Beat: relentless pursuit, resolve hardening.

chapters.title: The Rite Half-Erased
chapters.summary: In the tower, Sable discovers the rite's final line was destroyed deliberately: the binder becomes the Bell's keeper, bound to the village forever. Anselmo arrives begging her not to finish it. POV: Sable. Beat: the full price revealed at the worst moment.

chapters.title: Toll
chapters.summary: The Bell strikes for her. Sable sings the complete lament—twice—naming herself not as the promised victim but as the one who chooses, rewriting the ledger's last entry in her own hand. The chair empties. POV: Sable. Beat: climax; identity reclaimed through self-authorship.

chapters.title: Sunrise Over Corvo Alto
chapters.summary: Dawn. The villagers emerge to find the tower silent and Sable alive but changed—she can hear the Bell always now, a low keeping-note under every sound. The photographs show the table with one fewer chair. POV: Sable. Beat: survival's cost made visible.

chapters.title: A Room for the Bell
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Sable stays in the village as its reluctant keeper, recording the lament properly at last—with the whole truth in her liner notes. Teo helps her set a place at the table each night, not out of fear, but witness. POV: Sable. Beat: bittersweet resolution; loyalty and truth finally share a room.
